transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-11-26 15:00 PT | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Jordan, Priya, Samir (Redwood) - Maya, Ravi, Lena (Quantaco)

[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): okay hey everyone thanks for joining, quick check-in on the POC cost econ workstream. we pushed the updated spreadsheet this morning, link in the calendar.
[00:10] Maya (Quantaco): yes saw it, thanks. we want to focus today on tokens per second per dollar, and like real caching savings when we turn on prefix cache, not just theoretical.
[00:20] Priya (Redwood SE): yep, we ran two sets of tests last week: baseline hosted g4-equivalent run with no caching, and then with prefix/KV caching enabled. numbers are rough-ish because traces vary but baseline throughput was ~1,200 tokens/sec per GPU and cost translate to about 0.00045 $/token for the session; with caching we saw effective tokens/sec/$ improve to ~1,900 tokens/sec per GPU which is roughly a 55% lower unit cost for repetitive prefixes.
[00:45] Ravi (Quantaco): those are promising. can you repeat that, the tokens/sec/$ math? the spreadsheet column B to F i wasn't sure which assumptions you used for tokenization.
[00:55] Jordan: sure - assumptions: 1 model replica (A100-ish equivalence), steady-state load, avg request length 350 tokens, prefix reuse rate we assumed 40% for chat workload and 70% for the embed-ish batch. pricing assumptions are in tab 'assumptions' - we can adjust.
[01:15] Priya: important nuance - tokens/sec per dollar depends heavily on the cache hit rate and KV-savings for KV-cache cold-start. in our cache bench the KV hit rate for the chat trace ended up around 48% after 6 hours, not the 70% optimistic number. with 48% hit we still improved unit cost by ~35%.
[01:40] Maya: ok that aligns with what we see on our side; users often repeat a small set of prompts. what about batching? in some runs you recommended batch size 32 and sometimes 64, what's the p99 impact?
[01:55] Samir (Redwood): good question - batching increases throughput (more tokens/sec) but adds tail latency. from our microbench: immediate throughput gains from batch 8 -> 32 were ~2.3x, 32 -> 64 gave another ~1.3x. p50 latency is fine, p99 for 64 at shorter sequences jumps by ~200-300ms depending on model and kv cache interaction. So if you need strict p99 < 300ms, we'd recommend smaller batches or low-latency routing.
[02:30] Ravi: and quantization? we tried int8 vs int4 - how does that change tokens/sec/$ and quality?
[02:40] Priya: quantization helps. int8 gives a decent throughput bump (~1.4x) with minimal quality drop for most tasks; int4 can give ~2x throughput but quality regressions sometimes occur on generation diversity. our recommended path in POC: start with int8 for non-critical tasks, run evals on your safety/health prompts before moving to int4. cost numbers in spreadsheet reflect int8 baseline.
[03:05] Lena (CTO): when you say "cost" are you including network egress and storage for caches? we need full econ to compare to our internal on-prem fleet.
[03:15] Jordan: good call - spreadsheet has separate line items: compute (GPU hours), storage for cache (object store ~ negligible in our numbers but included), and network egress as a separate column - we can toggle those. for the hosted numbers egress was estimated at 0.02 $/GB. we can add a view that replicates your on-prem cost inputs.
[03:40] Maya: curious about cache cold-start behavior - we saw a big hit when a new user session is first served. does Redwood keep warm caches across replicas?
[03:50] Priya: by default KV-cache is per-replica; prefix cache can be shared via a redis layer in front but that adds some network hop. in a dedicated cluster we can co-locate caches to get faster warm starts; our bench shows steady-state after a day where hit-rate stabilizes. cold-start latency for an uncached prefix is just the generation time, nothing extra, but you lose the cost savings until it's cached.
[04:20] Ravi: can you run a 24-hour bench with our chat traces and measure hit-rate over time, and include hit-by-prefix frequency and avg saved tokens per hit?
[04:28] Priya: yes that's on our action list, we'll turn on the longer bench with the trace you provide, and share logs.
[04:35] Jordan: another area - autoscaling/burst vs reserved dedicated. for consistent high throughput dedicated capacity wins on unit cost; but if your traffic is spiky, autoscale with burst policies could be better monetarily. our modelling shows dedicated at ~30-45% lower cost for steady loads >X tokens/sec.
[04:55] Maya: what's X?
[05:00] Samir: roughly sustained 250k tokens/sec across all users; below that autoscale can be competitive depending on commit and burst rates. we'll surface the break-even in the updated sheet.
[05:15] Lena: security question - if we move to dedicated private, where do logs and KV-caches live and how are they encrypted?
[05:23] Jordan: in Redwood Private dedicated, KV stores and caches live in customer VPC by default, we integrate with KMS for encryption at rest and TLS in transit. we'll attach our security pack and SOC2/ISO statements in the follow-up.
[05:40] Maya: competitor question - we've had conversations with OpenAI on managed endpoints and Anthropic for chat models. how do you compare on unit cost?
[05:50] Jordan: high-level - managed endpoints tend to be simpler but unit cost higher for heavy usage; our goal is to give you tooling (caching, batching, quantization) to reduce unit cost while keeping an easy API. we'll add a competitor row in the spreadsheet with public list prices for apples-to-apples.
[06:10] Ravi: what's the expected error rate/regression risk when switching quantization or enabling aggressive batching? we worry about production quality dips.
[06:20] Priya: recommended guardrails: run diff-evals on a held prompt set (we can run these as part of POC), enable quality thresholds (auto-rollbacks), and keep canary traffic low on risky changes. historically regressions are uncommon with int8, more likely with int4 or extreme batching that affects decoding timing.
[06:45] Maya: ok - can you show a quick example from your bench where caching saved X tokens and reduced cost by Y?
[06:50] Priya: yes example: a support-chat flow with repeated salutations and context tokens we saw average saved tokens per session ~120 tokens, per-session cost drop around 22% in hosted tests. that scales for many sessions.
[07:10] Jordan: note also that semantic caching for embeds can reduce downstream compute by avoiding re-embedding ~ identical content; for your bulk embed jobs we saw 60-70% reuse on deduped traces which reduced tokens processed in model runs.
[07:30] Maya: great. any surprises in the bench?
[07:33] Priya: only that kv-hit plateaued lower than expected on one of your traces - looked like high variance in user prompts. we'll need broader traces to get a representative hit-rate.
[07:50] Ravi: timeline to decision? we want to decide if we go to dedicated by mid-December.
[07:58] Jordan: that's achievable: next week bench results + your traces, then a short cost review with finance. if numbers look good we can schedule a 1-week dedicated trial in the week of 2025-12-08.
[08:12] Lena: for the dedicated trial what constrains are there for peering and security?
[08:18] Samir: minimal: VPC peering, SAML/SCIM for SSO, and KMS integration. we'll send a checklist.
[08:25] Maya: okay let's recap next steps.
[08:28] Jordan: recap: Jordan sends cost model spreadsheet (with competitor comparison) by 11/28; Priya runs 24h cache bench and shares results by 12/01; Quantaco uploads three workload traces by 11/28; Ravi confirms VPC/security contacts by 11/30; schedule dedicated trial week if break-even looks good for week of 12/08.
[08:50] Maya: thanks all - appreciated.
[08:52] Jordan: thanks everyone. adjourn.
